item.title: You should observe the fish in the bathtub, rather than jumping in and swimming with them.
item.description: Understanding and Strategy of Stock Market Investment: Being a Spectator
item.content:encoded:
Cognition and Strategy in Stock Market Investment: Being an Observer

The most foolish thing an adult does is try to reason with others.

After deeply observing multiple stock trading groups, I have gained a deeper understanding of the essence of investment and the collective behavior in the market, forming my own investment principles and thoughts. The investment market is like a bathtub, where the fish swim around—noisy and chaotic. I realize that a true investor should not jump into the tub to swim with them, but rather stand at a higher level, observing calmly and planning rationally. Here are my thoughts:

I. Don’t jump in and swim with them; observe them

Stock trading groups are like a miniature market, filled with people driven by emotion—panic, greed, excitement, and disappointment. When I joined the groups and saw them passionately discussing various stocks and hot topics, I found:

  • Emotion drives their decisions: Many people do not base their decisions on rational analysis, but rather follow the crowd in chasing gains and selling losses.
  • Noise fills the market: Truly valuable information is rare; most discussions are merely emotional venting or repetition of information.

If I also get caught up in it, joining their discussions or sharing my own views, I will lose my clear head and instead be driven by their emotions, losing my ability to make independent judgments. Therefore, I tell myself:

You must observe the fish in the tub, not jump in and swim with them.

II. Stand at a Higher Level: Understand, Analyze, and Respond Steadily to the Market

Investing is a contest of self-cognition and patience, not a game of timing the market. To proceed steadily in the market, one must:

  • Stand at a higher cognitive level: View the market from a long-term, rational perspective, rather than being swayed by short-term fluctuations.
  • Understand market emotions and patterns: Observe changes in market sentiment and identify phenomena of irrational panic and excessive optimism.

But I will never try to predict the market’s peak or “perfectly time the top,” because that is speculation, and it is almost impossible to sustain success. Instead, I choose to:

  • Maintain balanced asset allocation: When the market rises irrationally, reduce positions moderately to achieve asset rebalancing.
  • Capture long-term value: When the market falls, and the fish panic, moderately increase holdings.

Don’t try to swim with them into your net; instead, place your net at the right spot from a higher level.

III. Don’t Participate in Discussions, Don’t Speak Up: Maintain the Role of the Invisible Observer

In the process of investing, I realized an important principle: Do not participate in discussions, do not speak up.

The Significance of Not Participating in Discussions:

  • Stay away from market noise, avoiding influence from others’ emotions and opinions.
  • Maintain independent thinking, avoiding cognitive bias and herd mentality.

The Benefits of Not Speaking Up:

  • Prevent the exposure of your own logic and strategy, guarding your advantage.
  • Avoid getting caught up in debates or counter-emotional reactions, which could disrupt your naturally calm state.

I choose to be an invisible observer, silently watching the group’s behavior and emotional fluctuations, finding patterns and opportunities within them, rather than being swept up in the clamor of the discussion.

IV. The Core Strategy: Long-Term Perspective, Rebalancing, and Patience

As an observer of the market, my strategy is:

Silently Observing Market Sentiment

  • Clearly seeing their panic and greed, seeing through their irrational behavior.
  • Treating the group’s discussions and actions as an “emotional indicator,” rather than a decision basis.

Maintaining Balanced Asset Allocation

When the market rises irrationally, reduce positions moderately to prevent asset proportions from becoming too high, thus rebalancing. When the market falls significantly, assess the true value and increase holdings appropriately, aligning with the long-term investment logic.

Adhering to Long-Term Investment Principles

  • Not chasing short-term gains, nor trying to precisely predict market timing.
  • Persisting with patience and discipline, holding quality assets long-term to reap the rewards of compounding over time.

The noise in the market will always exist, but the real opportunities belong to those who are calm, rational, and adhere to the principle of rebalancing.

V. Summary: Be a Rational Observer, Stay Away from Speculation

The investment market is like a large bathtub, where the fish swim around, and most people blindly swim along with the emotions and trends, eventually losing their way. I, however, choose to:

  • Observe, not participate: Stay away from the influence of the crowd’s emotions, maintaining a clear mind.
  • Maintain asset allocation and rebalancing: Adjust timely to ensure the asset structure aligns with long-term goals.

Execute silently, wait patiently: Harvest market returns with independent judgment and a long-term perspective.

The essence of investment is the victory of cognition and discipline, not the contest of speculation and impulse. Only by being an observer can you see more clearly and proceed more steadily.

item.title: Causes of Conformity
item.description: Explore the psychological reasons behind conformity behavior, including normative influence, self-confidence, and group pressure, and analyze how to resist the conformity effect.
item.content:encoded:
The purpose of conformity behavior is to avoid the complete loss of social support

When peers who hold the same dissent provide a certain level of social support, the loss of group social support is not so absolute. However, when the originally supportive peers abandon this participant and begin agreeing with the majority opinion, the power of the majority re-exerts its maximum efficacy—the rate of conformity rises again to 30%. Therefore, in the situation set up by Asch, the most primary force at work is undoubtedly normative social influence rather than informational influence.

Normative Influence

The key role of normative influence is also very obvious in other experiments. When participants are allowed to answer privately—meaning their answer will not be seen by the majority—the rate of conformity is much lower. If you like the people in the majority, you will certainly exhibit more conformity because you hope they like you rather than driving you out of the group.

Confidence Also Affects Conformity

When you are selecting fashion suitable for a certain event that matches your personal style, are you confident in your ability? If the answer is yes, you might be indifferent to street TV interviews about “this year’s trends.” However, those who lack confidence in their “sense of fashion” often quickly decide what new clothes to purchase based on these TV programs.

The Difficulty of Saying “No”

  • People conform both to maintain social acceptance and to increase the chance of acting correctly in uncertain situations.
  • The stronger these individual motivations, the stronger the group’s attraction and cohesion, the greater the pressure exerted by the group on the individual.
  • Because this pressure depends on how the individual reacts to the group, the individual cannot easily resist it.

If Hitler told you to shock a stranger, would you comply?

Milgram’s shock experiment tells us that human nature is willing to commit evil under command, even exceeding the command from above. This can also explain the behavior of sycophants, as releasing the evil of human nature simultaneously allows them to demonstrate loyalty and seek merit.

item.title: The principles of conduct are essentially the art of adaptation. How can one be dogmatic about a single aspect?
item.description: Exploring how to maintain the ability to be flexible and adaptable in a changing world, avoiding extreme thinking, while emphasizing the importance of the doctrine of the mean and an open mindset.
item.content:encoded:
The way of navigating life is also the art of adaptation; it cannot be rigidly fixed on one side.

Mistakes in the Last Assessment

  • My first speculative attempt, lacked consideration of the factor of project failure (or default).
  • We may need to continuously correct our judgments, because the world is changing.

Avoiding Extreme Thinking

  • Being biased toward one side means falling into extreme thinking, believing that a certain strategy or concept can apply forever, or holding an absolute view of certain things. This way of thinking ignores the complexity and diversity of reality. Navigating life and responding to change requires balance; one cannot be too aggressive, nor too conservative.
  • In economic decision-making, behavior biased toward one side may manifest as excessive reliance on a certain policy tool (such as monetary easing or fiscal stimulus), ignoring long-term side effects. Similarly, when individuals invest, if they relentlessly pursue a certain investment model, they may miss other potential opportunities.

Winning by Adapting to the Enemy

  • The world is full of uncertainty and variables, whether in politics, economics, or personal life. Facing these changes, rigidly adhering to a fixed strategy or concept will lead to mistakes, or even missed opportunities. Adaptation means adjusting one’s behavior and strategy according to environmental changes, maintaining flexibility and adaptability.
  • The “Winning by Adapting to the Enemy” mentioned in Sun Tzu’s Art of War also emphasizes the importance of responding to change. Whether facing the battlefield or various challenges in life, the ability to adapt to change often determines success or failure.

Balance and Moderation

  • The Doctrine of the Mean (Zhong Yong) emphasizes finding balance between extremes. True wisdom lies in knowing when to persist and when to change. This applies to life, career, investment, and politics. Timely adjustments not only avoid the difficulties brought by rigidity but also allow us to better seize new opportunities.
  • “Adaptation” is not blindly following change, but adjusting strategy according to the situation while maintaining core principles. This flexibility allows us to maintain direction while effectively meeting challenges.

Open Mindset

  • Responding to change also requires us to maintain an open mindset, always ready to accept new knowledge and new information. Often, success depends on whether we can timely recognize the arrival of change and take corresponding action. Those who always cling to old ideas and are unwilling to accept change are often eliminated during periods of flux.
  • In this age of information explosion, maintaining openness and critical thinking is necessary to avoid being misled and to quickly adapt to new situations and challenges.

All Animals Are Equal, But Some Animals Are More Equal Than Others

The absurd slogans and constantly revised rules are Orwell’s primary tools for exposing how totalitarian regimes manipulate, deceive, and suppress the masses through language. These slogans appear simple and easily understandable, aligning with the interests of the animals, but in reality, they are cleverly twisted and utilized by the rulers (the pigs). Ultimately, they betray the original intent of the revolution, plunging the other animals back into a state of oppression and exploitation.

Four Legs Good, Two Legs Bad

Absurdity: This was the animals’ original slogan, used to distinguish themselves (representing the proletariat and revolutionaries) from humans (representing the exploiters and rulers). This slogan emphasizes that all four-legged animals (as well as the two wings of birds) are superior to two-legged creatures (i.e., humans). However, as the pigs’ power gradually increased, they eventually learned to walk upright, and the slogan was subsequently changed (see the next point). Function: This simple and memorable slogan helped the animals unite against humans, but simultaneously, it overly simplified complex reality, failing to recognize the intricate hierarchies and evolving class struggles among the animals themselves.

Four Legs Good, Two Legs Better

Absurdity: As the pigs slowly imitated humans and gained more privileges after the revolution, they quietly changed the slogan to “Four Legs Good, Two Legs Better,” betraying the original revolutionary intent. This change reveals the process of power corruption, showing that the pigs gradually became indistinguishable from the enemy they initially overthrew (humans). Function: This new slogan symbolizes the pigs’ complete domination of the farm and their betrayal of the other animals. By changing the language and rules, they confuse the other animals about the facts, gradually accepting the pigs’ new rule.

All Animals Are Equal, But Some Animals Are More Equal Than Others

Absurdity: This is one of the most famous absurd slogans from Animal Farm. It originally came from the first of the Seven Commandments of Animalism, “All Animals Are Equal,” but as the pigs’ power grew, they modified it to “Some Animals Are More Equal Than Others.” This statement is clearly self-contradictory, because equality itself implies no difference, yet the phrase “more equal” reveals the inherent unfairness of reality. Function: This slogan reflects how the rulers (the pigs) established a new class system by masquerading as equality. Through this linguistic manipulation, they make the other animals accept their subordinate status, while the pigs enjoy privileges.

Comrade Napoleon Is Always Right

Absurdity: Napoleon is the leader among the pigs, gradually becoming a dictator. This slogan implies that any action taken by Napoleon is flawless, absolutely correct, and beyond question. It is a typical totalitarian strategy that asserts the infallibility of the leader, thereby suppressing any dissent or criticism. Function: This slogan eliminates the space for opposition and questioning by promoting the absolute authority of the leader, causing the other animals to blindly follow him, regardless of how absurd or selfish his decisions may be.

Work Harder, Comrade Napoleon Is Right

Absurdity: This slogan is often repeated by a horse named “Boxer.” He believes that problems will eventually be solved through working harder, and that Napoleon is always correct. This blind loyalty and self-sacrifice reflect the trust of the common laborers (symbolizing the working class) in the ruling class, even when the ruling class is constantly exploiting them. Function: By promoting the values of labor and sacrifice, the rulers use this slogan to make the other animals work tirelessly without questioning the distribution of power or the injustice of the system.

Don’t Believe What You See, Believe What You Hear

Absurdity: This phrase is used by Napoleon’s propagandist, “Squealer,” to tell the animals not to trust the facts they see with their own eyes, especially when those facts contradict the party’s propaganda. This is similar to the concept of “doublethink” described by Orwell in 1984, which requires people to ignore reality and accept the false explanation provided by the rulers. Function: This slogan aims to distort the animals’ perception of reality, preventing them from questioning the pigs’ actions or decisions. This is a typical method used by totalitarian regimes to maintain their power by manipulating information and propaganda.

  1. Reputation is the cornerstone of power. With reputation alone, you can intimidate others and win victories. Once your reputation is damaged, you will find yourself in a position of helplessness, surrounded by enemies.
  2. Learn to dig into the corners of your enemy’s reputation to destroy them. Once the opponent’s reputation is damaged, you merely need to watch coldly and let public opinion seal their fate.

  1. Your assistants will be forgotten, but you will be remembered. Never do things yourself that others can do for you.

  2. You don’t need to say much; actions are more convincing, more likely to gain support, and more powerful.

  2. Everyone admires the bold and fearless; no one respects or admires the timid.

Power Law 29: Consider Everything, Plan to the End

  1. Your plan must have a beginning and an end; you must consider the issues around the outcome.
  2. Only by thinking further ahead can you dominate destiny and determine the future.

  1. In the long run, appearing crude or low-class will lead others to look down on you, or even disrespect you.
  2. Your behavior must constantly display the demeanor of a monarch and confidence in power, making others believe that you are the one destined to wear the crown and become king.

Power Law 35: Learn the Art of Controlling Time

  1. You must make others feel that you are always patient, as if you know that everything will naturally come to fruition.
  2. A hurried manner reveals that you lack control over yourself and cannot control time.

Power Law 36: Scorn What You Cannot Have; Ignoring It is the Best Revenge

  1. The more energy you invest in an enemy, the stronger they become. If there is something you love dearly but cannot obtain, show it complete disdain. The less interest you show, the more superior you appear.

Power Law 37: Create Unforgettable External Displays

  1. Use external displays to dazzle the crowd, and then no one will notice exactly what you are doing.
  2. Eye-catching portraits and grand symbolic postures will cultivate an atmosphere of power, and the crowd will inevitably respond to it.
  3. Enhance your charisma with striking images and radiant features, making others feel that your presence is extraordinary.

Power Law 38: Ideas Can Be Free, But Actions Must Conform to the Masses

  1. Your creativity can only be shared with friends who are tolerant of your character and who will appreciate your uniqueness.
  2. If you show signs of resisting the times, flaunting your unconventional ideas and non-traditional thinking, people will assume you are merely trying to attract attention and look down on them.

Power Law 39: Stir the Pond to Catch Fish

  1. Anger and loss of control are counterproductive strategically; therefore, you must always remain calm and objective. If you can provoke the enemy while remaining calm yourself, you have gained a decisive advantage.

Power Law 40: Scorn the Free Lunch

  1. Things offered for free are dangerous; they usually contain a trick or hide a potential obligation; therefore, valuable things are worth paying for.
  2. Paying full price is the smartest move, because excellence means no shortcuts.

Power Law 41: Try to Avoid Inheriting the Legacy of Great Figures

  1. If you inherit the legacy of a great figure or a famous parent, it means you must achieve more than twice the results of the former to surpass them in the public eye.
  2. Change direction and build your own reputation and identity.

Power Law 42: Attack the Shepherd, and the Sheep Will Scatter

  1. Problems often trace back to individual individuals—people who like to exaggerate, subordinates who are arrogant and unreasonable.
  2. Only by isolating or banishing them can you reduce their influence. By directly attacking the source of trouble, the blindly following masses will scatter.

  1. People are products of habit. Too much innovation brings trauma, leading to resistance.

Power Law 46: Don’t Appear Too Perfect

  1. The most dangerous thing is appearing flawless. Jealousy will breed silent enemies.
  2. Let others dissolve their jealousy into your small flaws, making you seem more human and approachable.
  3. Only God and the dead can achieve a state of perfection, and they are not punished by others.

Power Law 47: Don’t Exceed Your Target; Learn to Stop at the Right Time in Victory

  1. Under the excitement of victory, arrogance and overconfidence will push you beyond the original goal.
  2. Once you go too far, the enemies you create will be more numerous than the opponents you defeated.
  3. Set a goal, and when the chariot of victory arrives, stop immediately.
  4. When you succeed, remember that you must be cautious even when retreating from victory.
  5. The moment of victory is the most intoxicating, but it is also the most dangerous.

Power Law 48: Conform to Change, Let the Intangible Overcome the Tangible

  1. The best way to protect yourself is to flow like water and have no fixed shape.
